why.correct: Inherited potential is expressed through the environment. Nature and nurture work together rather than one alone.
options: Right: the same inherited potential led to different heights in different environments.
The famine clearly changed the outcome, so heredity alone does not set height.
Both brothers inherited a tendency to be tall; inheritance still matters.
The stem says both inherited the same tendency; the environment differed.

why.correct: Heritability is the share of the variation among people in a particular group and environment that is linked to genetic differences. It says nothing about how much of one person’s trait comes from genes.
options: Heritability is not about the makeup of any one person’s trait.
Right: heritability describes variation within a group.
A heritable trait can still change a great deal with the environment.
Heritability is not the share of people who have a trait.

why.correct: Plant the same mix of seeds in rich and poor soil. Within each field, height differences are mostly genetic; the difference between the fields is entirely the soil. Heritability within groups says nothing about the cause of differences between them.
options: Heritable traits can change with nutrition, schooling and much else.
The method does not matter; the point is what heritability describes.
Right: two fields of the same seeds in rich and poor soil differ because of the soil.
Neither part of this holds; both sources vary at both levels.

why.correct: Evolutionary psychology explains behavior and mental processes by how they helped our ancestors survive and reproduce, through natural selection.
options: The behavioral perspective explains behavior by what a person learned from consequences in their own lifetime.
The humanistic perspective stresses growth and free choice.
The sociocultural perspective looks at the influence of culture and other people.
Right: it explains a trait by its survival and reproduction advantages.

why.correct: In natural selection, inherited variations that improve survival and reproduction are passed on more often, so they spread through a population over many generations.
options: Right: those traits are passed on more often.
Traits acquired during a lifetime, such as stronger muscles, are not inherited.
Natural selection is not a choice by any individual.
Selection works over many generations on inherited variation, not on what is useful today.

why.correct: Eugenics tried to "improve" humanity by controlling who could have children. It treated poverty and lack of schooling as inherited defects and led to forced sterilization and, in Nazi Germany, mass murder.
options: Evolutionary psychology studies shared human traits; it does not rank groups or justify sterilization.
Right: it ignored the environment and violated human rights.
Natural selection describes what happens over generations, not what anyone should do.
Twin studies show that both genes and environment matter, and a heritable trait is not fixed for life.

why.correct: In an adoption study, resemblance to the biological parents points to heredity, and resemblance to the adoptive parents points to the shared environment.
options: Adoption placements are not made by researchers or at random; this is a correlational design.
They share a home with their adoptive family.
Right: so each source of similarity can be compared separately.
No one manipulates who is adopted, so adoption studies are correlational.

why.correct: In twin studies, both kinds of twins grow up together. Identical twins share all their genes, fraternal twins about half; when identical twins are more alike, genes are contributing.
options: Fraternal twins share both genes and a womb and are the same age, so this mixes heredity and environment.
Here genes are the same and the home differs, so this comparison is about environment.
This changes both genes and home at once, so neither can be singled out.
Right: the home is shared in both, so the extra likeness tracks the extra genes.

why.correct: Because adoptive siblings share no genes, their similarity points to the shared environment: the same home, books and schools.
options: Right: genetically unrelated children raised together are still somewhat alike.
If they were, unrelated siblings would show about zero correlation.
Adoptive siblings are not biologically related.
A positive correlation means the siblings are alike, not that their scores are low.

why.correct: Separated twins shared a womb, are the same age and are often placed with similar families. These shared environments can inflate their similarity, which is why researchers combine several designs.
options: A correlation shows a relationship, not that each individual’s reading is caused by genes.
Right: separated twins are often placed in similar families and communities.
Identical twins share all their genes, wherever they are raised.
The correlation is +0.72, positive and strong.

why.correct: Twin and adoption data together show that both heredity and environment contribute to differences in the trait.
options: Supported: more shared genes go with more similar scores.
Supported: unrelated adoptive siblings are somewhat alike, and twins raised together are more alike than twins raised apart.
Not supported: environment matters, and heritability says nothing about a fixed outcome.
Not supported: fraternal twins share about half, like other siblings.
Not supported: identical twins raised apart still correlate +0.72.

why.correct: A case study looks in depth at one person. It can suggest ideas, here that diet changes the course of PKU, which later studies of many children confirmed.
options: No twins were compared.
No adoptive and biological families were compared.
Right: an in-depth report on one child.
A correlational study measures variables across many people; this followed one child.

why.correct: PKU is the classic example of heredity and environment interacting: an inherited condition whose harm depends on what the child eats.
options: The diet changed the outcome dramatically.
PKU is inherited; the diet changes what the inherited condition does.
The study is about one inherited condition; it says nothing about how often intellectual disability is inherited.
Right: the same inheritance leads to very different outcomes with different diets.

why.correct: Inherited is not the same as fixed. Newborn screening and a special diet let children with PKU develop typically, which is why screening is routine.
options: Right: inherited does not mean unchangeable.
Untreated PKU is very harmful.
People with PKU keep the condition; the diet manages it.
The condition itself is inherited; both matter.

why.correct: An interaction answer names the inherited part, the environmental part, and how the outcome depends on both.
The somatic nervous system, part of the peripheral nervous system, carries commands from the central nervous system to the skeletal muscles and brings in sensations from the body.
options: Right: it controls voluntary movement of the skeletal muscles.
The parasympathetic division calms the body; it does not move skeletal muscles.
The autonomic system runs automatic functions such as heart rate, not deliberate movement.
The sympathetic division arouses the body’s organs; it does not direct the dive itself.

why.correct: The sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system speeds the heart and breathing, widens the pupils and slows digestion, preparing the body to act.
options: The parasympathetic division calms the body, slowing the heart.
Right: it arouses the body for action.
The somatic system moves skeletal muscles; these are automatic changes in organs.
The heart and breathing changes are carried out through the peripheral, autonomic system.

why.correct: The parasympathetic division conserves energy: it slows the heart, lowers blood pressure and lets digestion resume.
options: The sympathetic division arouses the body and slows digestion.
Digestion and heart rate are automatic, not voluntary movement.
Right: it calms the body and supports digestion.
The spinal cord is part of the central nervous system; the calming of organs is autonomic.

why.correct: The spinal cord carries messages between the brain and the body. An injury cuts off the parts of the body whose nerves connect to the cord below it.
options: The spinal cord is part of the central nervous system.
Losing feeling and movement is about blocked messages, not calming.
Both arms and legs are moved by the somatic system.
Right: the nerves for the arms join the cord above the injury.

why.correct: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. Everything else, the nerves reaching out to the body, is the peripheral nervous system.
options: Right: the brain and spinal cord make up the CNS.
The brain is the center of the central nervous system.
Nerves that run the heart belong to the autonomic system.
Nerves that move skeletal muscles belong to the somatic system.

why.correct: Neurons are the basic building blocks of the nervous system: cells specialized to receive and send information. The next topic follows how they fire.
options: That describes the somatic nervous system.
Right: neurons are the cells that send messages.
That describes the spinal cord.
Neurons are cells found throughout the nervous system, not one brain part.

why.correct: Breathing is one autonomic function people can also control on purpose. Slow breathing is associated with a shift toward parasympathetic, calming activity.
options: Sympathetic activity would speed her heart, not settle it.
The heart is run by the autonomic system, not the somatic.
Right: slow breathing is linked to calming responses.
The calming of her heart is carried out by the peripheral, autonomic system.

why.correct: The peripheral nervous system divides into the somatic (voluntary) and autonomic (automatic) systems.
options: Those two are the divisions of the autonomic system.
Those make up the central nervous system.
The central nervous system is separate from the peripheral.
Right: both branch from the peripheral nervous system.

why.correct: The sympathetic division prepares the body for action: faster heart, wider pupils, slower digestion, more sweating.
options: Right: the diagram lists both under the sympathetic division.
Those are parasympathetic effects.
Kicking a ball is somatic.
That is the role of the central nervous system.

why.correct: The heart’s pounding is sympathetic (autonomic) arousal; jumping back moves skeletal muscles through the somatic system.
options: This swaps the two: the heart is autonomic and the jump uses skeletal muscles.
Right: an automatic arousal and a voluntary-muscle movement.
The parasympathetic division calms the heart rather than speeding it.
The jump uses skeletal muscles, moved by the somatic system.

why.correct: After a threat passes, the parasympathetic division brings heart rate and breathing back down.
options: Heart rate is not under somatic control.
The sympathetic division raised his heart rate.
Right: it calms the body after arousal.
The calming of the heart is carried out by the parasympathetic division.

why.correct: The line jumps from about 70 to 110 just after the noise at 60 seconds.
options: That happens later, as the heart rate recovers.
There is a sharp rise after the noise.
The rise is sudden, followed by a slow fall.
Right: the peak comes at 90 seconds.

why.correct: Once the surprise passes, parasympathetic activity slows the heart back toward its resting rate.
options: Right: heart rate returns toward rest.
Sympathetic arousal raised the heart rate after the noise.
Heart rate is controlled by the autonomic system, not the somatic.
Nothing was blocked; the body returned toward rest.

why.correct: The noise came at 60 seconds and the heart rate was back near 72 at 240 seconds: about three minutes. Arousal is fast; calming takes longer.
options: At 90 seconds the heart rate was at its peak, 110.
Right: it is about 72 at 240 seconds, close to the resting 70.
At 120 seconds it was still about 98.
It fell to about 72 by 240 seconds.

why.correct: Apply each division to the part of the graph it explains, with the numbers.
A marks a dendrite, the branching fiber that collects incoming signals and passes them to the cell body.
options: Right: A is a dendrite, which receives messages from other neurons.
C is a segment of myelin sheath, which insulates the axon; it does not receive messages.
D is an axon terminal, where the neuron sends its message out, not where it receives one.
E is the synaptic gap, the space between two neurons, not a part of the receiving cell.

why.correct: C is the myelin sheath. Myelin lets the action potential jump quickly down the axon; when it is damaged, as in multiple sclerosis, signals slow, scramble or stop, which causes weakness, numbness and vision problems.
options: Right: damaged myelin slows or blocks signals traveling down the axon.
Reuptake happens at the axon terminal and synapse, not at the myelin.
Dendrites receive signals; multiple sclerosis attacks the myelin on the axon.
The cell body keeps working; the problem is how fast the signal travels.

why.correct: A drug that occupies or blocks receptors so the neurotransmitter cannot act is an antagonist: it weakens that neurotransmitter's effect.
options: Right: blocking the receptor stops the neurotransmitter from working, so the drug is an antagonist.
An agonist mimics or boosts a neurotransmitter; this drug stops it from acting.
A reuptake inhibitor keeps neurotransmitter in the gap longer; it does not block receptor sites.
A hormone is a chemical messenger carried in the blood, not a drug that blocks a receptor.

why.correct: The return trip is reuptake. A drug that blocks it (a reuptake inhibitor) leaves more neurotransmitter in the synaptic gap, so the message to the receiving neuron is stronger and longer.
options: Right: blocking reuptake leaves more neurotransmitter in the gap for longer.
Release happens before reuptake; blocking reuptake does not reduce how much is released.
Receptors stay in place; with more neurotransmitter around they are used more, not lost.
Reuptake has nothing to do with myelin, which insulates the axon.

why.correct: Threshold is about -55 mV. Below it nothing fires; at or above it the neuron fires a full action potential. There is no partial action potential (the all-or-none principle).
options: Right: -62 mV is below a threshold of about -55 mV, so the neuron does not fire.
There are no small action potentials: firing is all-or-none.
Action potential speed depends on the axon (such as myelin), not on how strong the input was.
The refractory period follows an action potential; this neuron never fired.

why.correct: Because each action potential is all-or-none, a neuron cannot make a single signal bigger. A stronger stimulus makes neurons fire more often and recruits more neurons.
options: Right: intensity is coded by firing rate and the number of neurons firing.
All-or-none: every action potential is the same size, whatever the stimulus.
The path from her hand to the spinal cord is the same length for the mug and the stove.
A neuron does not switch neurotransmitters to signal a stronger stimulus.

why.correct: Rest, threshold, the action potential down the axon, release at the terminal, binding across the synapse, then reuptake clears the gap.

In a reflex arc the sensory neuron carries the message into the spinal cord, an interneuron passes it on, and a motor neuron moves the muscle. The brain gets the message a moment later, which is when he feels the pain.
options: Right: sensory neuron in, interneuron in the spinal cord, motor neuron out.
This runs the arc backward: sensory neurons carry information in and motor neurons carry commands out.
The spinal cord handles the reflex without waiting for the brain, which is why the foot moves before the pain is felt.
Interneurons sit in the brain and spinal cord, not in the foot.

why.correct: In myasthenia gravis the immune system attacks acetylcholine receptors at the junction between nerve and muscle, so muscles weaken with use.
options: Right: myasthenia gravis blocks acetylcholine signals to muscles.
Multiple sclerosis damages myelin in the brain and spinal cord, not the receptors on muscles.
Dopamine is involved in movement planning and reward; the muscle receptor here is for acetylcholine.
Multiple sclerosis damages myelin, and serotonin is not the muscle neurotransmitter.

why.correct: A drug that binds to a neurotransmitter's receptors and triggers the same effect is an agonist. Opioid pain medicines work this way at endorphin receptors.
options: Right: Drug E mimics endorphins at their receptors, so it is an agonist.
An antagonist would block the receptors and stop pain relief, the opposite of what Drug E did.
The summary says Drug E binds to receptors, not that it slows reuptake.
Drugs that mimic endorphins are opioids, which slow the nervous system; stimulants speed it up.

why.correct: An experiment manipulates the variable (which pill) and randomly assigns participants, so the groups start out alike and the pill is the likely cause of the difference.
options: Right: manipulation plus random assignment is what allows a cause-and-effect conclusion.
Volunteering at one clinic describes who was studied; it does not support a causal claim.
The rating scale is how relief was measured (the operational definition), not why a causal conclusion holds.
A larger sample helps, but without random assignment the groups could still differ in other ways.

why.correct: Placebo 55 minutes minus Drug E 20 minutes is 35 minutes sooner.
An operational definition says exactly how this study measured the variable: minutes until the self-rated pain score dropped below 4.
options: Right: relief was measured as minutes until the 0 to 10 rating fell below 4.
Feeling better is the concept in general; it does not say how it was measured.
Which pill a patient took is the independent variable, not the measure of relief.
Brain endorphin activity was never measured in this study.

why.correct: With repeated use the brain adapts to a drug, so the same dose has less effect: tolerance.
options: Right: needing more of a drug for the same effect is tolerance.
Withdrawal is the unpleasant symptoms when a drug is stopped; these patients were still taking it.
Reuptake is how a neuron takes back its own neurotransmitter; it does not explain a growing dose.
The refractory period is a brief pause after one action potential, measured in milliseconds.

why.correct: Slowing reuptake means serotonin stays in the synaptic gap longer and keeps reaching the receptors. That is what a reuptake inhibitor does.
options: Right: a reuptake inhibitor keeps serotonin available in the synapse.
Blocking receptors would make the drug an antagonist and weaken serotonin's effect.
Adrenaline is a hormone from the adrenal glands; this drug acts on serotonin at the synapse.
Motor neuron firing controls muscles; the drug changes serotonin, which is linked to mood.

why.correct: Ghrelin is released by an empty stomach and signals hunger to the brain.
options: Right: ghrelin rises before meals and makes people feel hungry.
Leptin, released by fat cells, signals that the body has enough stored energy; it reduces appetite.
Melatonin rises in the dark and helps time sleep, not hunger.
Oxytocin is linked to bonding, childbirth and nursing, not mealtime hunger.

why.correct: Endorphins are the body's natural painkillers; strenuous exercise can raise them, easing pain and lifting mood.
options: Right: endorphins reduce pain and can lift mood.
Substance P carries pain signals, so more of it would increase the pain.
Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter, not a natural painkiller.
Acetylcholine makes muscles contract; it does not explain pain relief.

why.correct: GABA is the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter: it makes neurons less likely to fire. A drug that boosts GABA slows the nervous system, so it is a depressant.
options: Right: boosting the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA slows the brain, as a depressant does.
Stimulants speed up the nervous system; GABA slows neurons, and glutamate is the excitatory one.
Hallucinogens distort perception; alcohol boosts GABA rather than blocking it.
Opioids act at endorphin receptors; the stem says alcohol works through GABA.

why.correct: Adrenaline (epinephrine) is a hormone released by the adrenal glands into the blood during danger. It speeds the heart and breathing, and because the blood carries it, the effect lasts longer than a single neural signal.
options: Right: adrenaline prepares the body for an emergency and keeps it aroused for minutes.
Melatonin helps time sleep; it would make her drowsy, not alert.
Leptin signals fullness; it is not part of the emergency response.
Serotonin is a neurotransmitter linked to mood and sleep, not a blood-borne alarm signal.

why.correct: Oxytocin is a hormone released during childbirth, nursing and close contact and is linked to bonding. An early study reported more trust after a nasal spray, but later, larger studies did not reliably reproduce a simple trust effect.
options: Right: the bonding link is real; the "trust spray" claim has not held up reliably.
Pain signaling involves substance P and endorphins; oxytocin is a hormone linked to bonding.
Ghrelin signals hunger; oxytocin is linked to bonding and birth.
The early finding was not reliably replicated, so "proven" overstates the evidence.

why.correct: Time = distance / speed = 0.9 / 60 = 0.015 seconds, which is 15 milliseconds. Without myelin, at about 1 meter per second, the same trip would take most of a second.
Cocaine does not add dopamine. It blocks reuptake, so the dopamine the neuron already released lingers in the synapse.
D is Broca's area, in the lower left frontal lobe. Damage there leaves understanding mostly intact but makes producing speech slow and effortful (Broca's aphasia).
options: Right: D is Broca's area, which helps produce speech.
E is Wernicke's area; damage there harms understanding, and speech stays fluent but makes little sense.
B is the motor cortex strip; damage would weaken movement on the right side of the body, not specifically speech.
C is the occipital lobe, which processes vision.

why.correct: C is the occipital lobe at the back of the brain, where visual information is first processed.
options: Right: the occipital lobe handles vision, so pressure there disturbs sight.
Hearing is processed in the temporal lobe, below the lateral fissure.
Hand movement is controlled by the motor cortex strip at the back of the frontal lobe.
Planning depends on the front of the frontal lobe, the prefrontal area.

why.correct: B is the motor cortex. Movement commands cross over, so the left motor cortex moves the right side of the body (contralateral organization).
options: Right: the left motor cortex controls the right side of the body.
Control crosses: each hemisphere moves the opposite side, not the same side.
Each hemisphere has its own motor cortex for the opposite side of the body.
B is the motor cortex, in front of the central sulcus; touch is processed in the somatosensory cortex just behind it.

why.correct: F is the cerebellum, which coordinates movement and balance. Strength comes from the motor cortex, but smooth, timed movement needs the cerebellum.
options: Right: F is the cerebellum, which coordinates balance and smooth movement.
B is the motor cortex; damage would cause weakness, but this man's muscles are strong.
D is Broca's area, which helps produce speech.
A is the front of the frontal lobe, involved in planning and judgment rather than balance.

why.correct: In an experiment the researcher manipulates the variable and randomly assigns participants. Brain damage cannot ethically be assigned, so the study compares groups that already differ.
options: Right: nothing was manipulated or randomly assigned; the damage already existed.
Studying one hospital limits who the results describe, but a one-site study can still be an experiment.
How speech was measured is the operational definition; it does not decide the method.
Informed consent is an ethical safeguard, used in experiments too.

why.correct: The frontal group spoke far fewer words (18 vs 92) but followed almost as many instructions (17 vs 18): production was hit hard, understanding barely. That pattern fits Broca's area.
options: Right: speech output dropped sharply while understanding stayed close to the other group's.
This reverses the result: understanding was nearly the same in both groups.
The two groups differed a lot in words per minute, so the damage location mattered.
Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe is also involved in language; the study does not show only one region matters.

why.correct: 92 minus 18 is 74 more words per minute.
The summary says names were replaced with code numbers, which keeps each patient's data confidential. It also describes review board approval and informed consent.
options: Right: replacing names with codes protects confidentiality.
The summary describes no deception, so there was nothing to debrief.
Random assignment is a design feature, not an ethical safeguard, and it was not used here.
No treatment was given; the summary does not describe this.

why.correct: Information on the left reaches the right hemisphere, which controls the left hand. With the corpus callosum cut, it cannot pass the information to the left hemisphere, where speech is in most people.
options: Right: the right hemisphere knows and the left hand shows it, but the speaking left hemisphere does not.
This has the sides reversed: a flash on the left goes to the right hemisphere, and the right hemisphere moves the left hand.
The hand picked the key reliably, so the right hemisphere did receive the picture.
Vision still works; only the link between the two hemispheres is cut.

why.correct: A few patients were studied in depth: case studies. They tell us a lot about each person, but these patients had unusual brains (years of severe epilepsy), so care is needed in generalizing.
options: Right: in-depth study of a few patients is a case study, and they may not be typical.
No one was randomly assigned to have the surgery; it was done for medical reasons.
Patients were tested on tasks, not asked questions about themselves.
Testing used a controlled screen in a lab, not observation in daily life.

why.correct: Split-brain studies show hemispheric specialization (language mostly left, some spatial tasks more right). Large brain-imaging studies find no evidence that people sort into these two types; both hemispheres work together through the corpus callosum.
options: Right: specialization is real, but people do not sort into the two types the magazine describes.
The studies tested what each hemisphere could do after surgery; they did not sort people into types.
The studies were of people with epilepsy, and even they did not show two types of thinkers.
In most people language is mainly in the left hemisphere, not the right.

why.correct: The medulla, at the base of the brainstem, controls breathing and heart rate. Damage there threatens life, so breathing must be supported.
options: Right: the medulla keeps breathing and heartbeat going.
The cerebellum coordinates movement; it sits behind the brainstem, not in it.
The hippocampus helps form new memories; it does not run breathing.
The occipital lobe handles vision.

why.correct: The hippocampus, deep in the temporal lobe, is needed to form new memories of facts and events.
options: Right: the hippocampus is needed to form new memories.
The amygdala is linked to fear and emotional reactions, not forming new memories of people.
The thalamus relays sensory information; her vision and description are fine.
The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance; her problem is with memory.

why.correct: The hypothalamus keeps the body in balance (homeostasis): it regulates temperature, hunger and thirst, and directs the pituitary gland.
options: Right: the hypothalamus maintains homeostasis, including body temperature.
The cerebellum coordinates movement; it does not set body temperature.
Broca's area helps produce speech.
The somatosensory cortex registers the feeling of cold on the skin but does not regulate temperature.

why.correct: The amygdala is a limbic structure that responds to threats; when both are damaged, fear reactions are blunted.
options: Right: the amygdala is central to fear responses.
Balance and coordination depend on the cerebellum.
Relaying sensory signals is the thalamus's job.
Language depends on Broca's and Wernicke's areas in the cortex.

why.correct: The reticular activating system runs through the core of the brainstem and controls arousal: waking, alertness and attention to the surroundings.
options: Right: the reticular activating system controls arousal and alertness.
The limbic system handles emotion, drives and memory, not basic wakefulness.
The reward center drives motivation and pleasure through dopamine.
Association areas in the cortex integrate information for thinking; they are not in the brainstem.

why.correct: fMRI tracks changes in blood oxygen, which rise where neurons are working, so it shows where activity happens. EEG records electrical activity from the scalp: excellent timing, poor location.
options: Right: fMRI shows where activity increases.
EEG is good at when activity happens but poor at pinpointing where, especially deep in the brain.
Lesioning destroys tissue; it is used in animal research, not to study healthy people viewing faces.
A case study follows one person in depth; it is not a way to map activity while people look at faces.

why.correct: Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to rewire, forming new connections and shifting functions to other areas. It is strongest in childhood.
options: Right: the remaining brain reorganized and took over functions, which is neuroplasticity.
Contralateral organization describes which side of the body each hemisphere controls, not recovery.
The all-or-none principle describes how a single neuron fires.
Specialization is the reason recovery is remarkable; the recovery itself is plasticity.

why.correct: The line reaches N3 in the first three to four hours and does not reach it after that. Deep N3 sleep is concentrated early in the night.
options: Right: N3 appears in the first half of the night and then fades.
In the last two hours the sleeper cycles between N2 and REM, with no N3.
N3 is bunched early, not spread evenly.
REM periods follow N2, not N3.

why.correct: REM periods start at about 1.3, 2.5, 4.1, 5.5, 6.8 hours, roughly every 90 minutes, and grow from 10 to 30 minutes.
options: Right: regular cycles of about 90 minutes, with longer REM periods later.
This reverses the trend: the last REM period is the longest.
There are five REM periods, not one.
They follow a regular cycle and their lengths increase.

why.correct: 110 / 480 = 0.229, which is about 23%. Adults typically spend about 20 to 25% of sleep in REM.
The researchers measured two variables as they occurred (screen minutes and sleep minutes) and computed a correlation. Nothing was manipulated and no one was assigned to use the phone more or less.
options: Right: two measured variables and a correlation coefficient make it correlational.
An experiment would assign students to different amounts of screen time; this study did not.
A case study examines one person or a few in depth; this study had 240 students.
The data came from phone apps and trackers, and the point was the relationship between two variables, which makes it correlational.

why.correct: A negative r means that as one variable goes up the other tends to go down. A size of about 0.4 is a moderate relationship.
options: Right: negative direction, moderate strength.
A negative correlation means the two variables move in opposite directions.
A correlation is not a percent and cannot show cause.
An r of -0.42 is clearly different from zero, so the variables are related.

why.correct: A third variable affects both measured variables. Heavy homework could make students stay up later (less sleep) and use their phones more before bed, creating the correlation on its own.
options: Right: homework could raise screen use and cut sleep at the same time.
The tracker is how sleep was measured (the operational definition), not a third variable.
Sample size does not create a relationship between the two variables.
The study length is part of the method; it does not drive both variables.

why.correct: An operational definition says how this study measured the variable: total minutes of sleep from the wrist tracker.
The body's roughly 24-hour clock, set mainly by light, takes days to shift to a new time zone. Until it does, his sleepiness follows home time.
options: Right: jet lag is a circadian rhythm out of step with local time.
Deep N3 sleep does not explain being awake at night and sleepy at noon.
Narcolepsy is a lasting disorder of sudden sleep attacks, not a result of travel.
He still cycles through both REM and NREM; the timing of sleep is off.

why.correct: Hypnagogic sensations, such as the feeling of falling and a sudden jerk, happen in N1, the light transition from waking to sleep.
options: Right: falling sensations and jerks come as you first drift off, in N1.
N3 is deep sleep later in the cycle; people are hard to wake from it.
In REM the major muscles are largely paralyzed, so a jerking leg is not typical.
N2 comes after N1; the falling feeling marks the very start of sleep.

why.correct: REM sleep combines an active, waking-like brain, rapid eye movements and near-paralysis of the major muscles. Vivid dreams are most common here.
options: Right: active brain, darting eyes and limp muscles define REM.
N3 shows large, slow delta waves, not fast waves.
N1 is light drifting-off sleep without rapid eye movements or muscle paralysis.
An awake person has normal muscle tone; limp muscles point to REM.

why.correct: Sleepwalking (somnambulism) happens during deep N3 sleep, which is why it occurs early in the night and is more common in children, who have more N3.
options: Right: sleepwalking arises from deep N3 sleep early in the night.
In REM the major muscles are largely paralyzed, so ordinary sleepwalking does not come from REM.
Narcolepsy is sudden sleep during the day, not walking at night.
REM sleep behavior disorder happens in REM, not N3, and involves acting out dreams.

why.correct: In REM sleep behavior disorder, the normal muscle paralysis of REM fails, so people act out their dreams. It is most common in older men.
options: Right: acting out a dream means REM paralysis has failed.
Sleepwalking comes from N3 and people rarely recall a dream.
Sleep apnea is repeated pauses in breathing, not acting out dreams.
Insomnia is trouble falling or staying asleep.

why.correct: In sleep apnea breathing repeatedly stops during sleep. Each pause briefly wakes the person to breathe, so sleep is broken and daytime sleepiness follows.
options: Right: pauses in breathing with gasping and loud snoring point to sleep apnea.
Narcolepsy is sudden attacks of sleep during the day, not pauses in breathing at night.
People with insomnia have trouble falling or staying asleep, but not pauses in breathing.
Acting out dreams is a REM problem, not pauses in breathing.

why.correct: Narcolepsy brings sudden, uncontrollable sleep attacks, often going straight into REM; strong emotions such as laughter can trigger a sudden loss of muscle tone.
options: Right: sudden sleep with a quick drop into REM is narcolepsy.
Sleep apnea causes tiredness from broken sleep, not sudden sleep in the middle of a conversation.
Sleepwalking happens at night in N3, not as sudden daytime sleep.
Insomnia is difficulty sleeping, not falling asleep without warning.

why.correct: Activation-synthesis says dreams start as random neural activity from the brainstem during REM; the cortex synthesizes it into a story, which is why dreams can be bizarre.
options: Right: random activation, then the cortex makes sense of it.
That is the consolidation view of sleep and dreaming.
That is the restoration theory, about why we sleep, not what dreams are.
Hidden-wish dream theories are outside this course and have little scientific support.

why.correct: Recalling more after a night of sleep supports the idea that sleep helps stabilize and store new memories (consolidation).
options: Right: better recall after sleep fits the consolidation view.
Restoring energy is a different function; the measure here was memory.
This finding is about memory, not where dreams come from.
The circadian rhythm times sleep but the study tested memory.

why.correct: Insomnia is persistent trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, with daytime effects, lasting months.
options: Right: long-lasting trouble falling and staying asleep is insomnia.
Narcolepsy is falling asleep suddenly, the opposite problem.
Sleep apnea involves breathing pauses, usually with loud snoring.
Sleepwalking happens during deep sleep; it is not lying awake.

why.correct: Looking straight at something focuses its image on the fovea, which is packed with cones, the receptors for color and sharp detail.
options: Right: the fovea, full of cones, gives the sharpest vision.
The blind spot has no receptors at all, so nothing there is seen.
The lens focuses light; it does not detect anything. Receptors are in the retina.
Rods at the edge detect dim light but not fine detail.

why.correct: Rods, which respond to dim light, are spread across the retina outside the fovea. Looking slightly away puts a faint image on rods instead of the cone-packed fovea.
options: Right: rods outside the fovea are better at detecting dim light.
Looking straight at the star puts it on the fovea; looking away moves it off.
Nothing is seen at the blind spot, because it has no receptors.
Where you look does not change how much light the lens gathers.

why.correct: The axons that form the optic nerve leave through one spot, so there is no room for receptors there. Light falling on it is not detected. We rarely notice because the other eye and the brain fill in the gap.
options: Right: no receptors means no detection at that spot.
There are no cones at the blind spot at all.
Light reaches the spot; there is simply nothing there to detect it.
The blind spot has no rods, so it cannot be overloaded by them.

why.correct: Transduction is the conversion of one kind of energy (here light) into neural signals. Rods and cones do it for vision; hair cells in the cochlea do it for hearing.
options: Right: turning light into neural signals is transduction.
Sensory adaptation is a drop in response to an unchanging stimulus.
Sensory interaction is one sense affecting another, as smell affects taste.
Signal detection theory explains whether a faint stimulus is reported, depending on expectations and stakes.

why.correct: A said "tone" more often in both kinds of trial: 46 hits and 18 false alarms, against B's 31 hits and 3 false alarms.
options: Right: A said "tone" more often, raising both hits and false alarms.
A had more false alarms (18) than B (3), not fewer.
B had fewer hits (31 vs 46) and fewer false alarms (3 vs 18).
The listeners differ a lot: 46 vs 31 hits and 18 vs 3 false alarms.

why.correct: Signal detection theory says detecting a faint stimulus depends on the stimulus and on the person's expectations and motives. A reward for hits made A say "tone" freely; a penalty for false alarms made B cautious.
options: Right: the payoff each listener faced changed their response, as signal detection theory predicts.
Adaptation would lower sensitivity to the static over time; it does not explain the different payoffs.
Weber's law is about noticing a change in a stimulus, not deciding whether a faint one is present.
Both listeners' ears transduce sound the same way; the difference is in their decisions.

why.correct: 46 hits out of 50 tone trials: 46 / 50 = 0.92, which is 92%.
Saying "yes" more readily catches more real signals (hits) but also flags more non-signals (false alarms), exactly as Listener A did.
options: Right: a lower bar for "yes" raises both hits and false alarms.
That is the cautious pattern of Listener B.
Raising hits while lowering false alarms needs a better signal, not a different decision rule.
Changing the decision rule does change the responses, as the table shows.

why.correct: Supertasters have more taste buds and taste bitter compounds, such as those in coffee and broccoli, much more strongly.
options: Right: strong dislike of bitter foods fits a supertaster.
Finding food bland suggests weaker taste, the opposite of a supertaster.
No longer smelling a steady odor is sensory adaptation.
Seeing colors with sounds is synesthesia.

why.correct: The researchers measured taste-bud counts and bitterness ratings as they were. Without manipulating a variable, the study shows a relationship, not cause, though a biological explanation is plausible.
options: Right: both variables were measured, not manipulated, so the study is correlational.
The coloring was applied for counting; it does not explain why the design cannot show cause.
The age of the participants limits who the results describe; it is not why cause cannot be shown.
A rating scale gives numbers; it does not affect whether cause can be shown.

why.correct: Umami is the savory taste detected by receptors for glutamate, found in broth, soy sauce, tomatoes and aged cheese.
options: Right: umami is the savory taste.
Oleogustus is the proposed taste of fat, not the savory taste of broth.
Gustation is the sense of taste as a whole, not one taste.
Olfaction is the sense of smell.

why.correct: Weber's law says the just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the original stimulus. 2 out of 100 is 2%; 2% of 400 grams is 8 grams.
options: Right: the same 2% of 400 grams is 8 grams.
2 grams is the same amount, but the difference needed grows with the size of the stimulus.
4 grams would be only 1% of 400 grams, which she would not notice.
20 grams is 5%, much more than she needs.

why.correct: The Weber fraction is 3 / 300 = 0.01. The just-noticeable difference for 900 Hz is 0.01 × 900 = 9 Hz.
With constant, unchanging stimulation, receptors and the nervous system respond less. That is sensory adaptation.
options: Right: an unchanging stimulus is felt less over time.
Transduction is converting energy into neural signals; it is still happening.
The absolute threshold is the faintest stimulus detected half the time; the cold is far above it.
Synesthesia is one sense triggering another, such as seeing colors for numbers.

why.correct: Much of what we call flavor comes from smell. When smell is blocked, taste alone is flat. One sense changing another is sensory interaction.
options: Right: losing smell changes taste, which is sensory interaction.
Adaptation is a drop in response to a constant stimulus, not a blocked nose.
Weber's law is about noticing changes in stimulus strength.
Signal detection is about deciding whether a faint stimulus is present; his soup is not faint, it lacks smell.

why.correct: Opponent-process theory says color is coded in pairs (red-green, blue-yellow). Staring tires the green side, so the white wall drives the red side more: a red afterimage.
options: Right: the paired red-green process explains the red afterimage.
Three cone types explain color matching and most color deficiency, but not opposite-color afterimages.
Place theory explains how we hear high pitches.
Gate control theory explains why pain can be blocked.

why.correct: Trichromatic theory says color vision depends on three types of cones. Missing or faulty red- or green-sensitive cones cause red-green color vision deficiency, which is inherited and far more common in men.
options: Right: a missing or faulty cone type causes red-green color deficiency.
Rods work in dim light and do not code color; missing rods causes night blindness.
Color signals go to the occipital lobe; the problem is in the cones.
The lens does not filter out red or green light.

why.correct: Prosopagnosia (face blindness) is an inability to recognize faces even though vision is otherwise fine.
options: Right: seeing faces but not recognizing them is prosopagnosia.
Blindsight is responding to things a person says they cannot see, after damage to the visual cortex.
Synesthesia is one sense triggering another.
Color deficiency affects colors, not recognizing faces.

why.correct: In blindsight, damage to the visual cortex removes conscious sight, but other brain pathways still process some visual information and guide behavior.
options: Right: responding to what one cannot consciously see is blindsight.
Prosopagnosia is trouble recognizing faces.
Adaptation is a reduced response to a constant stimulus.
Everyone has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the eye; it does not explain a stroke.

why.correct: Loud noise damages the hair cells in the cochlea, which do not grow back. Damage to the cochlea or auditory nerve is sensorineural hearing loss. Hair cells near the base, which respond to high pitches, are often hit first.
options: Right: noise damages cochlear hair cells, causing sensorineural loss.
Hair-cell damage is sensorineural; conduction loss is in the outer or middle ear.
A torn eardrum blocks sound before the cochlea: that is conduction loss.
Wax builds up in the ear canal, the outer ear, and causes conduction loss.

why.correct: Place theory: high pitches vibrate particular spots near the base of the cochlea. Frequency theory: for low pitches, neurons fire at the same rate as the sound wave. For middle pitches, neurons take turns firing (the volley principle).
options: Right: place theory for high pitches, frequency theory for low ones.
This reverses the two theories.
The volley principle extends frequency theory to middle pitches; place theory explains high ones.
Opponent-process theory explains color vision, not hearing.

why.correct: Gate control theory says the spinal cord has a neural "gate". Signals from rubbing travel on fast fibers and partly close it, so fewer pain signals reach the brain.
options: Right: rubbing sends signals that partly close the pain gate in the spinal cord.
Signal detection explains whether a faint stimulus is reported, not why rubbing eases pain.
Trichromatic theory explains color vision.
Frequency theory explains hearing low pitches.

why.correct: Phantom limb sensations show that pain is created by the brain. The brain areas that once served the leg remain active, so pain can be felt in a limb that is gone.
options: Right: pain is felt where no limb remains, so the brain generates it.
Kinesthesis senses the position of body parts that are there, using receptors in muscles and joints.
Adaptation reduces a sensation; here a sensation appears.
Synesthesia mixes senses; nothing is triggering one sense with another.

why.correct: The vestibular sense, from fluid-filled canals in the inner ear, tracks balance and head movement. After spinning, the fluid keeps moving briefly, so she feels motion.
options: Right: inner-ear fluid still moving after spinning makes the world seem to turn.
Kinesthesis senses the position of body parts from muscles and joints, not head rotation.
Adaptation would make a constant sensation fade, not create a feeling of motion.
Transduction happens in every sense; it does not explain the feeling of spinning.
